summary.text: A simple random sample is a group chosen from a larger population in a way that gives every individual the same chance of being picked.
Every subset of a given size has the same probability of being the chosen sample as any other subset of that size.
It requires a complete sampling frame and needs little prior knowledge of the population beyond that, which makes it simple to interpret.

facts.label: Equal chances
facts.value: Every subset of k individuals is equally likely to be chosen

facts.label: Without replacement
facts.value: Usually done without choosing any member more than once

facts.label: Needs a frame
facts.value: A complete sampling frame, which may be hard to build for large populations

facts.label: Benchmark role
facts.value: Textbooks use it without replacement to judge other sampling methods

items.prompt: Ten friends share six basketball tickets. Each gets a number from 1 to 10, and random numbers are drawn, skipping repeats, until six friends are named. Why is this fair?

options.label: Every possible group of six is equally likely to be chosen
Lower numbers are drawn first more often than higher ones
Friends who asked for tickets first get priority
Each friend is guaranteed a turn at a ticket

items.explain: In a simple random sample every set with the same number of items has the same probability of being chosen.

items.prompt: A teacher seats 30 students in 5 rows and 6 columns, then picks one column at random as her sample of 5. Every student has the same chance of being chosen. Why is it still not a simple random sample?

options.label: Some students are more likely to be picked than others
A single column is too small to count as a sample
Many groups of five students can never be chosen
Picking a column at random is not truly random

items.explain: Only groups arranged as one column can be selected, so not all subsets of five are equally likely, even though each student has the same chance.

items.prompt: A pollster draws 500 names from a population of millions. How much does it matter whether each name is put back into the pool after being drawn?

options.label: A great deal, since repeats would be very common
It cannot be done for a population that large
Putting names back is always the required method
Hardly at all, since drawing the same person again is unlikely

items.explain: For a small sample from a large population, sampling without replacement is approximately the same as with replacement, because the chance of picking the same individual twice is low.

items.prompt: A school numbers 1,000 students, picks a random starting number, then takes every 10th name for a sample of 100. Each student has the same chance of inclusion. Why is it still not a simple random sample?

options.label: The starting number was not chosen at random
Some sets of 100 students are far likelier than others
Every tenth name does not form a sample at all
Some students are more likely to be included than others

items.explain: Systematic sampling gives each unit the same chance of inclusion, but different sets of units have different probabilities, because the first pick fixes the rest.

items.prompt: A team knows almost nothing about a population except a full list of its members, and asking anyone is cheap. Which plan fits best?

options.label: Asking only the first names on the list
Cluster sampling, since it always beats simpler plans
A simple random sample, valued for its simplicity
Asking volunteers who come forward

items.explain: Simple random sampling best suits cases with little information about the population and cheap, easy data collection; otherwise stratified or cluster sampling may do better.

items.prompt: A researcher draws a simple random sample and finds it looks a bit unrepresentative of the population. What does that tell us?

options.label: The selection method must not have been random
A random draw does not guarantee any one sample is a perfect picture
Random sampling works only if repeated until the sample looks right
The population must be too large to sample

items.explain: Unbiased random selection means the average sample would represent the population, but it does not guarantee that a particular sample is a perfect representation.

paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: A simple random sample, or SRS, is a smaller group picked by chance from a larger population, with every individual given the same probability. The rule reaches beyond single people. Any set of k individuals is exactly as likely to become the sample as any other set of the same size. It is a basic kind of sampling and can serve as one part of more complex methods.

paragraphs.heading: A fair way to share tickets
paragraphs.text: Picture ten college students and only six tickets to a basketball game. To keep it fair, each student gets a number from 1 to 10. Random numbers are then produced by a computer or read off a table of random numbers. Any number outside 1 to 10, or already drawn, is skipped, and the first six valid numbers name the winners.

paragraphs.heading: With or without replacement
paragraphs.text: Usually nobody may be picked twice, which is called sampling without replacement. Sampling with replacement is possible but less common, and it is normally named in full. Draws without replacement are no longer independent, yet most results of mathematical statistics still hold. When a small sample comes from a large population, the two methods are almost the same, since picking one person twice is unlikely. Survey textbooks use SRS without replacement as the yardstick for judging how efficient other methods are.

paragraphs.heading: What it promises
paragraphs.text: Unbiased random picking matters because, across many samples, the average sample would mirror the population accurately. That does not make any one sample a perfect copy. What it does allow is reaching conclusions about the whole population from the sample.

paragraphs.heading: Strengths and limits
paragraphs.text: SRS needs a complete sampling frame, which may not exist or may be impractical to build for a large population. Its strengths are that it avoids classification error, needs little prior knowledge of the population beyond the frame, and gives data that are easy to interpret. It fits best when little is known about the population, or when sampling is cheap enough that simplicity matters more than efficiency. Even with a complete frame, extra knowledge about the units can allow more efficient methods, and when those conditions are not met, stratified or cluster sampling may be the better choice.

paragraphs.heading: Equal chances are not enough
paragraphs.text: Any method that gives each unit the same chance of selection is called equal probability sampling, or epsem. Every SRS is epsem, but not every epsem sample is an SRS. Suppose a teacher whose class sits in 5 rows of 6 columns picks one column at random to get 5 pupils. Each pupil had the same chance, yet most groups of 5 could never be chosen, because only whole columns qualify.
